description: A fragrant, much-branched aromatic herb 30-90 cm tall with softly hairy stems, oval toothed leaves and purplish-green flower spikes (manjari). Grown in courtyards and homes across India.
cultural_significance: Revered in Hindu households as the earthly form of Goddess Lakshmi/Vrinda; worshipped daily at the Tulsi Vrindavan and offered in Vishnu worship. Not a Vedic-era plant by name, its prominence grows in the Puranas and later Nighantus.
habitat: Warm, sunny, well-drained soil; cultivated in courtyards, temples and gardens; naturalised in waste ground across the tropics.

uses.title: Cough, cold and bronchial congestion
uses.detail: Leaf juice or decoction with honey and ginger is a classical household remedy to loosen phlegm and ease cough; it is described as Kapha-Vata hara.

uses.title: Fever and seasonal infections
uses.detail: Decoction (kwatha) of leaves with black pepper is traditionally given in fevers and malaria-like periodic fevers.

uses.title: Stress and adaptogenic support
uses.detail: Modern studies on Ocimum tenuiflorum extracts suggest anti-stress and mild blood-sugar-lowering effects; evidence is preliminary.

classical_refs: Charaka Samhita - listed among Svasahara/Hikkanigrahana herbs

preparations.name: Swarasa (fresh leaf juice)
preparations.method: Crush fresh leaves and press out the juice; traditionally taken with honey.
preparations.note: Typical household use is small quantities; follow a practitioner's advice.

preparations.name: Kwatha (decoction)
preparations.method: Boil leaves with water (often with ginger and black pepper) until reduced; strain and sip warm.
preparations.note: Commonly used for coughs and colds.

preparations.name: Tulsi tea
preparations.method: Steep a few fresh or dried leaves in hot water for 5-7 minutes.

precautions: May lower blood sugar and slow blood clotting, so people on diabetes or anticoagulant medicines should consult a doctor. Avoid medicinal quantities in pregnancy. Traditionally said to reduce fertility in very high long-term use. Leaves are not chewed in some traditions due to their mercury-like heat, a cultural rather than clinical rule.

cultivation.water: Moderate; keep slightly moist, avoid waterlogging
cultivation.propagation: Seeds or stem cuttings; sow in spring or monsoon
cultivation.harvest: Pinch tips regularly; harvest leaves before flowering for best aroma

fun_fact: Tulsi is commonly planted in a raised Tulsi Vrindavan in Indian courtyards and is among the few plants folk-worshipped daily.

regions.name: South Asia (Widely cultivated)
regions.note: Courtyards, temples and gardens across the Indian subcontinent

regions.name: Gangetic Plains
regions.note: Naturalised in waste ground and cultivated everywhere
